Instrument names in scores mix several languages and several centuries. Some are misleading, and one
of them (the German "B") can make you play every note a semitone wrong.

## 1. BB♭, CC and E♭ tubas

Tubas are named by the length of their open tube, given as the note of its fundamental:

| Name | Built in | Size |
|---|---|---|
| **F tuba** | F | bass tuba (about 12 ft of tubing) |
| **E♭ tuba / E♭ bass** | E♭ | bass tuba (about 13 ft) |
| **CC tuba** | C | contrabass (about 16 ft) |
| **BB♭ tuba / BB♭ bass / "double B"** | B♭ | contrabass (about 18 ft) |

The doubled letter comes from an old English way of naming octaves, where the octave below the bass staff
was written with double capitals: CC, DD … BB. "BB♭" means the low B♭, telling the contrabass apart from a
smaller instrument "in B♭" such as the euphonium.

**What that means for reading.** In orchestras, wind bands and most of the world, **every tuba reads bass
clef at concert pitch**. The F, E♭, CC or BB♭ is only which instrument you hold; the player learns each one's
fingerings. In British-style brass bands the E♭ and BB♭ basses read **treble clef** as transposing
instruments: the E♭ bass sounds an octave and a major 6th below written, the BB♭ two octaves and a major
2nd below.

## 2. Names that mislead

| Name | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Cor anglais / English horn** | An alto oboe in F. Not English, not a horn. |
| **Tenor horn** (UK) = **alto horn** (US) | The same E♭ brass instrument, named for its part in the band. |
| **Baritone** | In the UK a smaller-bore B♭ brass instrument next to the euphonium; in the US often the euphonium itself; also a saxophone and a voice. |
| **French horn** | Just "horn" in scores and to horn players. |
| **Basso / alto** after a horn key | Which octave: horn in B♭ basso sounds a major 9th below written, B♭ alto a major 2nd below. |
| **Bass clarinet in B♭** | Same key as the clarinet, an octave lower, and see the treble/bass clef question in [lesson 2](score-multi-clef.qmd#the-octave-traps). |
| **Piccolo trumpet in B♭** | Sounds a minor 7th *above* written, an octave above the ordinary B♭ trumpet. |

## 3. Note names in other languages

Scores keep the composer's language. German letter names are the most dangerous, because they look like ours:

| English | German | French | Italian |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | C | ut / do | do |
| D | D | ré | re |
| E♭ | Es | mi bémol | mi bemolle |
| E | E | mi | mi |
| F | F | fa | fa |
| G | G | sol | sol |
| A♭ | As | la bémol | la bemolle |
| A | A | la | la |
| **B♭** | **B** | si bémol | si bemolle |
| **B** | **H** | si | si |
| F♯ | Fis | fa dièse | fa diesis |
| D♭ | Des | ré bémol | re bemolle |

So **"Klarinette in B"** is the B♭ clarinet, **"Horn in H"** is horn in B natural, and **"Trompete in Es"** is
the E♭ trumpet. German adds *-is* for sharp and *-es* (or just *-s*) for flat. French scores say *en ut*
(in C), *en si bémol*; Italian ones *in Do*, *in Si♭*.

Common instrument names: *Horn / Corno / Cor*, *Trompete / Tromba / Trompette*, *Posaune / Trombone*,
*Fagott / Fagotto / Basson*, *Kontrabass / Contrabbasso / Contrebasse*, *Bratsche / Viola / Alto* (French
"alto" is the viola!), *Englischhorn / Corno inglese / Cor anglais*.
